overview:
Ayogi-kevali (also spelled *ayogī-kevalin*) is a technical term in Jain philosophy describing a very brief, final stage in the spiritual progression of an omniscient being. In both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions, the term refers to a kevalin—one who has attained *kevala-jñāna* (perfect, infinite knowledge)—who is no longer engaged in any bodily activity (*yoga*). The word breaks down as *a-* (without), *yogi* (activity or bodily operation), and *kevali* (the omniscient one). Thus, an ayogi-kevali is an omniscient being whose bodily functions have completely ceased.

In the Jain *gunasthāna* system, which maps the soul’s ascent through fourteen stages, the ayogi-kevali corresponds to the fourteenth and final stage. At this point, all passions (*kaṣāyas*) have been destroyed, all activity of body, speech, and mind has ended, and the remaining non-destructive karmas are in the final moments of dissociation. The duration of this state is extremely short—described in the canonical texts as lasting only for a fraction of a second (one *samaya*). After this infinitesimal interval, the soul becomes a *siddha*, a liberated being residing at the apex of the universe (*siddha-śilā*).

Digambara texts emphasize that the ayogi-kevali has no physiological activity whatsoever: no breathing, no speech, no movement, and no mental operations. Śvetāmbara texts agree on the cessation of activity but differ slightly in describing the micro-temporal mechanics of the final karmic dissociation. Despite these nuances, both traditions affirm that the ayogi-kevali is the final embodied moment of an omniscient being before liberation.

The concept is central to Jain karma theory because it illustrates the complete cessation of *yoga*, which is the mechanism through which karmic influx (*āsrava*) occurs. When yoga ends, no new karma can bind, and the remaining karmas fall away automatically. The ayogi-kevali thus represents the culmination of the Jain path: perfect knowledge, perfect conduct, and the final release from all karmic matter.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra 10.2
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmi
primary_sources.notes: This sutra is the most frequently cited canonical definition. The Digambara and Śvetāmbara commentaries agree that this refers to the final moment of embodied existence when all bodily activity ceases.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra 10.3–10.4
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmi
primary_sources.translation: “When all karmas are destroyed, the being becomes a siddha.”
primary_sources.notes: Commentaries explain that the ayogi-kevali state is the immediate precursor to becoming a siddha, lasting only one samaya.

primary_sources.title: Gunasthāna descriptions in Digambara and Śvetāmbara canonical literature
primary_sources.author: Various (e.g., Kundakunda, Pūjyapāda; Śvetāmbara canonical redactors)
primary_sources.translation: “The ayogi-kevali is situated in the fourteenth gunasthāna.”
primary_sources.notes: Both traditions place the ayogi-kevali at the final stage of spiritual development, though they differ slightly in the technical description of the dissociation of the last karmas.

misconceptions.myth: Ayogi-kevali is a long-lasting or meditative state similar to deep samadhi.
misconceptions.reality: Primary texts state that the ayogi-kevali state lasts only one samaya—an extremely brief moment—before the soul becomes a siddha.

misconceptions.myth: Ayogi-kevali continues to perform subtle mental or spiritual activities.
misconceptions.reality: Jain doctrine holds that all activity (body, speech, and mind) ceases completely. No new karma can bind, and the remaining karmas fall away automatically.

misconceptions.myth: Only one Jain tradition recognizes the ayogi-kevali stage.
misconceptions.reality: Both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions affirm the ayogi-kevali, though they offer slightly different technical explanations of the final karmic dissociation.
